program.description: IEEE and the IEEE Standards Association launched the programme on 17 January 2023 to give free access to selected IEEE standards on AI ethics and governance; its page on IEEE Xplore now lists 12, each a PDF offered at no cost. The page says the standards are free thanks to its sponsors and names TÜV SÜD as a partner, and IEEE's launch release credits support from IEEE SA, industry sponsors and government. program.origin: Eleven of the twelve standards the programme lists are in IEEE's 7000 series, which grew out of the IEEE Global Initiative on Ethics of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems, launched in April 2016; the Initiative's members were encouraged to recommend standards projects to IEEE. IEEE credits the Initiative's report Ethically Aligned Design (first released in December 2016, revised in 2017 and 2019) with inspiring over twelve standards working groups, and says the P7000 series addresses issues the report identified; the Initiative's 2020 FAQ singles out P7012 among 'our IEEE P7000 Standards Working Groups'. IEEE SA records the authorisation (PAR approval) of the P7000 project on 30 June 2016, six months before the report's first version, and of P7012 on 6 December 2017. The twelfth standard, IEEE 2089-2021, is not in the 7000 series.
program.latestNote: No longer. When Doc Searls wrote on 29 January 2026 that MyTerms was 'the latest one', IEEE 7012-2025 (published on IEEE Xplore on 20 January 2026) was the most recently published of the standards the programme now lists. On 12 June 2026 IEEE published IEEE 7014.1-2026, Recommended Practice for Ethical Considerations of Emulated Empathy in Partner-Based General-Purpose Artificial Intelligence Systems, which the programme page now lists. As of 23 September 2026 it is the latest in the series by publication date; 7012-2025 is second. (The '-2025' in 7012's designation is its approval year; it was published in 2026.)

relation.summary: IEEE 7002-2022 is addressed to organisations: its scope 'defines requirements for a systems engineering process for privacy-oriented considerations' in products, services and systems that use employee, customer or other external users' personal data, and 'extends across the life cycle from policy through development, quality assurance, and value realization'. It gives procedures, diagrams and checklists so that users can perform a conformity assessment on their own privacy practices, and it describes privacy impact assessments (PIAs) as a tool for finding where privacy controls are needed and confirming they are in place. IEEE 7012-2025 is addressed to the individual: its purpose is 'to provide individuals with means to proffer their own terms respecting personal privacy' that machines operated by others can read and agree to, so that individuals can 'operate as first parties in agreements with others', mostly companies, which act as second parties. So 7002 sets requirements for an organisation's own engineering process, while 7012 covers how a person and a service provider select and sign a contract from a public roster kept by a neutral non-commercial entity, with a record kept by both sides.
relation.crossReferences: No. IEEE Std 7002-2022 never cites or mentions IEEE 7012, P7012 or any other IEEE 7000-series standard or project, and it never mentions the 7000 series, the IEEE Global Initiative or Ethically Aligned Design: clause 2 says there are no normative references, and a search for every form (7012, P7012, 7000, 7001, 7003, 7004, 7005, 7006, 7010, 7014, P70, IEEE 70, IEEE Std 70) finds only its own number, plus ‘7001’ and ‘7005’ inside ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27005:2018, which are ISO/IEC information-security standards, not IEEE 7001 or 7005. The only other IEEE-numbered documents it names are the networking standard IEEE Std 802.1Q-2014 and six joint ISO/IEC/IEEE systems and software engineering standards (15288, 12207, 16085, 24748-3, 24765 and 24774), all listed in the informative bibliography; 802.1Q, 15288 and 24774 are also recommended reading in the body (7.1, 9.2, 6.3). 7012 does not mention 7002 either, so the two standards are silent about each other in both directions. The clearest link the texts show is personal: John Wunderlich, vice chair of the 7002 working group, is the only person listed in both working groups. Two balloters, Werner Hoelzl and Piotr Karocki, appear in both balloting groups, and 7002’s ‘Randy K. Rannow’ may be 7012’s balloter ‘R. K. Rannow’ (not confirmed).
relation.otherPublicLinks: No public IEEE SA or working-group statement was found that relates 7012 to 7002 directly, or says that one builds on or complements the other. The P7012 PAR could not be read: the PAR PDF linked from IEEE SA's 2018 statement returns HTTP 401. What IEEE's public pages do show: (1) Different origins. IEEE SA's standard pages list 7002 under the IEEE Computer Society, 'C/S2ESC - Software & Systems Engineering Standards Committee', working group 'PDP - Personal Data Privacy Working Group', PAR approved 2016-12-07; and 7012 under the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology, 'SSIT/SC - Social Implications of Technology Standards Committee', working group 'MRPT-WG - Machine Readable Privacy Terms', PAR approved 2017-12-06. (2) The same series. IEEE SA's 2018 statement 'Our Role in Addressing Ethical Considerations of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS)' says that members of the IEEE Global Initiative 'are encouraged to recommend Standards Projects to IEEE based on their work', then lists both P7002 and P7012 among the 'approved IEEE Standards Projects', and refers to 'the associated IEEE 7000™ series of standards'. It says P7002 'specifies how to manage privacy issues for systems or software that collect personal data' by 'defining requirements that cover corporate data collection policies and quality assurance'. Of P7012 it says: 'Note that the purpose of this standard is not to address privacy policies, since these are one-sided and need no agreement. (Terms require agreement; privacy policies do not.)' The same statement says of the AI agent in a third project, P7006 (Personal Data AI Agent), that it is 'Designed as a tool to allow any individual to essentially create their own personal “terms and conditions” for their data'; P7006 is not in the GET series. (3) The Ethically Aligned Design, First Edition Overview (IEEE Global Initiative, 2019) calls the P7000 series 'the first series of standards in the history of the IEEE Standards Association that explicitly focuses on societal and ethical issues associated with a certain field of technology'. It lists P7002 as 'Inspired by The Personal Data and Individual Agency Control Committee, and supported by IEEE Computer Society' (as are P7004, P7005 and P7006), and P7012 only as 'Supported by IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology', with no EAD committee named. (4) IEEE SA's Autonomous and Intelligent Systems page (the IEEE SA link in the GET series sponsor list) lists 'IEEE P7002™ IEEE Standard for Data Privacy Process' under Related Standards but, as fetched on 2026-09-23, not 7012. (5) IEEE SA's Industry Connections page for the 'MyTerms' roadmap activity describes 7012 on its own and does not mention 7002 or the 7000 series.

reading7002.contrast: IEEE 7002 describes a privacy process run by the organisation: it identifies its own privacy requirements, assesses and responds to risk, sets procedures for data subjects' rights requests, and treats the public privacy policy as something the organisation 'publishes to notify potential data subjects of how data may be processed'. Where it names the parties to an agreement or contract, they are vendors, suppliers, partners and other third parties, or people inside the organisation; the individual is never one of them. IEEE 7012 starts from the other side: the individual, as first party, proffers standard terms, and the organisation accepts them, answers with a single alternative from the same list, or rejects them; identical copies of any agreement are kept by both sides, and a rejection is recorded. 7002 does not address who writes the terms: it gives the person no way to set, signal or agree terms, and mentions consent only once, to note that some jurisdictions do not recognise employee consent as valid authorisation.

findings.answer: 7002 is addressed to organisations. Its Abstract names 'Organizations and projects' that develop products and systems involving personal information as the 'candidate users' of the standard, and its scope says it 'applies to organizations and projects' of that kind (cl. 1.1); the 'users' who perform a conformity assessment with it are those organisations. The person first appears in the scope as a source of data: the process concerns systems 'utilizing employee, customer, or other external user’s personal data' (cl. 1.1). Almost every actor in the text sits inside the organisation or beside it: entities (an individual, group or function) holding the privacy roles (cl. 6.3), the entity accountable for the privacy framework (cl. 6.5), an 'authorized individual' whom the organisation identifies to accept risk (cl. 3.1, 8.1), security and privacy teams (cl. 7.3), control assessors (cl. 8.2.3), and outside parties such as vendors, suppliers, partners, contractors, regulators and law enforcement (cl. 6.2, 8.1). The data subject is defined only as the 'Natural person to whom personal data relates' (cl. 3.1), and privacy risk as the likelihood and impact that 'individuals or organizations will experience problems' from the data (cl. 3.1). In the requirements, the data subject is someone the organisation identifies and plans for. Organisations shall identify the types of data subjects (end-users, customers, employees) 'affected by' each policy (cl. 6.2, shall). They shall have policies and procedures covering data subjects' rights and how rights requests are handled (cl. 6.2, shall). The data map shall record the mechanism by which data is processed, with 'if the data action is visible to the individual' given as an example (cl. 7.3.1, shall; the visibility point is an e.g.). The individual's legal right to deletion becomes a capability the system supports (cl. 7.3.2, given as an example, though worded with shall). The person also serves as a yardstick: the 'Privacy needs of customers or service users' are an example of a contextual factor (cl. 5.3, Table 1, in the 'Third party relationships' column); one aspect of fairness 'can be evaluated' by whether data is processed for purposes that 'the user would have predicted or expected' (cl. 7.3.2, explanatory); one kind of control 'provides the individual with more control over how data is processed' (cl. 8.2.1, descriptive); developers of systems for others 'should consider' contextual factors that may affect the users of their system (cl. 4.2, supporting information); and the Introduction, which is not part of the standard, expects the process to 'increase end user satisfaction related to privacy'. 7002 gives the individual no task in the process itself. Cl. 4.2 says managing privacy risk requires 'active engagement' from a diverse set of stakeholders 'including' developers, business strategy, compliance and risk staff, senior leadership, designers, producers, suppliers and marketers (supporting information). The list is open, but data subjects, customers and end users are not among those listed. Risk acceptance involves 'relevant stakeholders', decided by an authorised individual, and in some instances 'external stakeholders, such as a partner or regulator' (cl. 8.1, shall and may). The risk assessment clause, including its passage on PIAs and DPIAs (cl. 7.4), says nothing about consulting data subjects; where 7002 suggests consulting anyone, it is 'those with experience in the field' during control selection (cl. 8.2.1) or legal advisers (cl. 5.2). The text sets up no feedback, complaint or participation channel for data subjects beyond the procedures for rights requests, and the nearest it comes to individual choice is the cl. 8.2.1 control that gives the individual 'more control'. The definitions of 'stakeholder' ('having a right, share, claim, or interest in a system') and 'privacy requirements' ('stakeholders’ desired privacy outcomes') are broad enough to include data subjects, and cl. 7.3 requires 'Wider stakeholder mapping' for each system, but the text never names data subjects, customers or end users as stakeholders. In 7002 the individual is notified and has legal rights the organisation must be able to handle, but is given no part in the process. How the passages are classed: cl. 1.3 defines 'shall' as mandatory and 'should' as recommended ('may' is permission, 'can' is possibility). The Introduction, which is not part of the standard, places the normative requirements in cl. 5–9 and says cl. 1–4 'provide supporting information'. Footnote 9 says notes in text, tables and figures are 'for information only', and Annexes A and B are marked informative. Sentences in cl. 5–9 without shall or should are treated here as explanatory, not requirements. (One list item in cl. 8.1 says 'Approval of stakeholders and ongoing monitoring is required' without 'shall'; the 'shall' later in the same clause covers the same ground.)

findings.answer: 7002 does not itself require a published privacy policy, and it prescribes no content for one. What it requires (cl. 6.2, shall) is that the organisation's own policies and procedures cover, among a minimum list of topics, 'Notice': the information the organisation provides on its processing and 'to whom and how the notice will be made available'. It then distinguishes those internal policies from 'an organization’s public privacy policy, which an organization publishes to notify potential data subjects of how data may be processed'. This is explanatory text, not a requirement. It recommends that where the two overlap they 'should not be contradictory' (should), and notes that some organisations publish internal policies too. In each case the organisation publishes the policy and decides to whom the notice goes, and the data subject is the one notified. 7002's definition of 'policy' faces inward: statements 'to condition the decisions made within an organization' (cl. 3.1). Annex A.2 (informative) points to examples of privacy policies 'published online': Kantara Initiative guidance on privacy policy topics, Intel's internal policy rules, and Cisco's Global Privacy Policy. In cl. 8.1 (explanatory), 7002 says that 8.3 looks at how risk 'can be shared, for instance through amending a privacy notice'. Clause 8.3 does not in fact mention notices, and 7002 does not explain how amending a notice shares risk or with whom. Its own description of 'Transfer/sharing' in the same clause is reassigning accountability 'to a third-party willing to accept the risk', such as a service provider. In that one sentence, then, the notice is presented as one of the organisation's tools for responding to risk. 7002 gives the individual no part in shaping it.

findings.answer: 'Consent' occurs once in the whole text, front matter included. The figures, which are images, were also viewed, and none mentions it. The one occurrence is in the cl. 6.2 minimum list of policy topics, in the 'Basis and purposes' item: an inline sentence beginning 'Note' that says 'some jurisdictions do not recognize employee consent to be a valid authorization for the use of employee data, in connection with employer organizational requirements.' It has no shall or should and imposes nothing. The item itself requires a policy on 'The legal basis and purposes' of processing (shall) and recommends that it include 'the rationale for the legal basis(es) selected' (should). So consent appears only in connection with the legal basis the organisation selects, and the single mention is a caution about relying on it for employees. 7002 says nothing about how consent is asked for, given, recorded, refused or withdrawn. The words opt-in, opt-out, withdraw, preference and choose do not occur. 'Choice' occurs once, about 'The choice and order of actions' in applying the standard, not about a person's choice.

findings.answer: No agreement or contract in 7002 is made with the individual. Where the text names the parties, they are outside businesses or people inside the organisation; in two passages the parties are not named. (a) Cl. 6.2 (shall, minimum policy topic): 'Third parties, e.g., vendors and suppliers', meaning the policies guiding 'data sharing agreements and contracts with vendors, suppliers, partners, contractors, and other third parties'. (b) Cl. 7.3 (shall): the system analysis must cover 'Wider stakeholder mapping', including where 'Service Level Agreements (SLAs) or other specific agreements such as data use contracts, exist or are needed'. The parties are not named. (c) Cl. 7.3 (explanatory): 'mutually agreed SLAs for the engagement with the accountable authority', a role cl. 6.3 places within the organisation. This is an internal arrangement. (The sentence opens 'As stated in 6.2', but cl. 6.2 does not mention SLAs.) (d) Cl. 5.3, Table 1 (examples): 'Contractual obligations' and the cascading of obligations to sub-contractors, listed under 'Third party relationships'. Figure 1, an image, labels this factor 'Third party relationships (e.g. contracts)'. (e) Cl. 8.1 (shall): accepting a risk needs an authorisation process in which 'relevant stakeholders are included to agree to that decision', and an authorised individual of the organisation makes the determination. Sometimes this includes 'a partner or regulator' (may). (f) Cl. 8.1 (explanatory): risk transfer or sharing means reassigning it 'to a third-party willing to accept the risk'. (g) Cl. 4.1 (supporting information): confidential data is described as 'agreed upon access restrictions', with the parties unspecified. 'SLA' also appears in the acronym list (cl. 3.2). The data subject is never a party to any agreement or contract in 7002. The word 'terms' appears in the sense of vocabulary ('key terms', 'in engineering terms'), in the idiom 'in terms of the cost' (cl. 8.2.1), and in IEEE's patent-licensing front matter (licence 'terms and conditions'), never as terms of an agreement with a person. The front matter's other mentions of licences and contracts (patent licensing, a photocopying licence, a liability disclaimer) are IEEE boilerplate, not part of the process.

findings.answer: No. 7002 does not mention machine-readable privacy terms or preferences, privacy signals, user agents or software agents, Do Not Track, Global Privacy Control, consent receipts, cookies, browsers, opt-in or opt-out, negotiation, or terms proffered by the person. The extracted text and the figure images were both searched. 'Agent', 'machine', 'preference', 'cookie', 'browser', 'track', 'receipt', 'negotiat-' and 'proffer' do not occur at all. 'Signal' occurs once, in 'a signal of increased privacy risk' (cl. 7.3.2). 'Global Privacy' occurs only in the name 'Cisco’s Global Privacy Policy' (Annex A.2). 'Consent' occurs once (see question 3). 7002 also does not mention IEEE 7012 or P7012, or any other 7000-series standard. The only number of that form in the text is its own. The nearest points are capabilities on the organisation's side. Cl. 7.3.2 gives NIST's 'Manageability' objective ('granular administration of data including alteration, deletion, and selective disclosure') as 'One example' of privacy engineering objectives, and ENISA's 'intervenability' goal as an additional perspective. The next sentence says 'These goals should be seen not as specific principles or requirements, rather these are suggested capabilities'. It follows the ENISA goals directly, and the text does not say whether it also covers the NIST objectives. Neither passage says who administers or intervenes. Cl. 8.2 gives 'allowing data to be amended' as an example of a functional requirement, and cl. 8.2.1 notes that one kind of control 'provides the individual with more control over how data is processed' (descriptive). Cl. 6.2 requires policies and procedures for handling data subjects' rights requests (shall), and cl. 7.3.2 gives deletion as an example of a legal right for which 'the system shall support capabilities' (an example worded with shall). Annex A.2 cites the Kantara Initiative, but only for 'guidance on certain key privacy policy topics'. In every case the organisation designs the mechanism. Nothing in 7002 lets the person set, send or agree terms.

findings.answer: IEEE 7002 describes a privacy process run by the organisation: it identifies its own privacy requirements, assesses and responds to risk, sets procedures for data subjects' rights requests, and treats the public privacy policy as something the organisation 'publishes to notify potential data subjects of how data may be processed'. Where it names the parties to an agreement or contract, they are vendors, suppliers, partners and other third parties, or people inside the organisation; the individual is never one of them. IEEE 7012 starts from the other side: the individual, as first party, proffers standard terms, and the organisation accepts them, answers with a single alternative from the same list, or rejects them; identical copies of any agreement are kept by both sides, and a rejection is recorded. 7002 does not address who writes the terms: it gives the person no way to set, signal or agree terms, and mentions consent only once, to note that some jurisdictions do not recognise employee consent as valid authorisation. (Careful wording for the site: 7002 does not describe the public privacy policy as 'terms', does not require one to be published, and does not claim to be about who writes the terms. The contrast is between what each standard contains, not an argument that 7002 rejects 7012's model. Clause 5.2.1.3 of 7012 has the individual's agent specify that the chosen terms 'shall supersede any Terms of Use (TOU) or Privacy Policy'.)

hew1973.answer: Yes, though only in informative Annex A.1 and without naming the report. The first example of existing privacy principles is the Fair Information Practices, ‘First developed by the US Government in 1973’. Footnote 13 reads ‘The first set of FIPs can be found here:’, followed by https://www.justice.gov/opcl/docs/rec-com-rights.pdf. That file is the Justice Department’s copy of the HEW report Records, Computers, and the Rights of Citizens (July 1973), the same file the site already cites. 7002 never names HEW, the Secretary’s Advisory Committee or the report’s title. It presents the OECD principles as ‘Building on the US Government’s initial work on FIPS’ and hands the rest of the history to a paper by Robert Gellman, linked by URL only (footnote 12). The FIPPs also appear, undated, as the ‘e.g.’ example in the cl. 3.1 definition of organisational privacy requirements. Annex A.1 illustrates the recommendation in 5.3.1 to adopt principles from widely used sources, and 6.2 separately requires policies that cover ‘The privacy principles adopted by the organization’. 7002 does not require the FIPs themselves.
